q: How do we roll back a failed deploy, and how long does it take?
reference: Run `deployctl rollback --to <previous-sha>`. Traffic flips back to the previous colour within about 20 seconds while that colour is still warm (30 minutes after a release); after that a rollback is a full release of the old sha and takes about six minutes.

q: Who gets paged for a SEV1 and when does it escalate?
reference: PagerDuty pages the primary on-call for any SEV1 or SEV2. The secondary is paged after 10 minutes without acknowledgement. A SEV1 lasting more than 30 minutes escalates to the engineering manager.

q: When should we fail over the database, and when should we not?
reference: Fail over when the primary is unreachable for more than 60 seconds, or when replication lag exceeds 5 minutes with the primary saturated. Do not fail over for a single slow query; kill the query instead.

q: What are the exact steps to renew a TLS certificate by hand?
reference: 1. Rotate the DNS provider token in the secrets vault (`vault write dns/token`). 2. Re-run the job: `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/acme-renew acme-manual`. 3. Confirm with `openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 | openssl x509 -noout -dates`.

q: Why did the Redis failover log everyone out, and what was changed afterwards?
reference: Sessions lived in Redis; the failover promoted a replica that had lost the last 40 seconds of writes and the session keyspace was not replicated with wait semantics, so every logged-in customer was logged out at 14:03 UTC on 2025-05-30. Sessions were moved to signed, encrypted cookies (ADR 0003, shipped 2025-11-05).

q: What does the blue-green deployment cost us, and why was it adopted?
reference: It doubles API capacity for 30 minutes after every release, about $340 per month. It was adopted after two incidents in February 2025 where rolling deploys let a bad build serve traffic for eleven minutes; blue-green makes rollback one command under 20 seconds.

q: How do I turn a feature off quickly?
reference: Flip its flag in the config service; it takes effect within ten seconds (10-second cache). Flags are no longer environment variables; every flag has an owner, description and expiry, and the `flags-audit` CI job fails on expired flags.

q: What are the rate limits for public and partner API keys, and what happens if Redis is down?
reference: Public API keys: 1000 requests per minute; partner keys: 10000 per minute; the login endpoint: 10 attempts per minute per IP. Limits are token buckets per API key in Redis at the API gateway; a Redis outage fails open (no limits) and pages the on-call.

q: What must happen to the old primary after a database failover, and why?
reference: It must be rebuilt from a fresh base backup before it rejoins as a replica; reusing its data directory caused the split-brain incident of 2024-11-08.

q: What was decided at the platform sync on 2026-09-01?
reference: The read-only MySQL instance is switched off on 2026-09-15, with its last backup kept for one year. (Status items: selective CI job skipping in review, web-only builds at 6 minutes with a 4-minute target; the search index rewrite proposal was accepted on 2026-08-25.)

q: How do I get a database password?
reference: Never copy one from a colleague; run `vault read db/creds/orders`, which gives a credential that expires in 8 hours.

q: What changed in the API in August 2026?
reference: On 2026-08-14 `GET /orders` gained `?since=` and `?until=` filters (also that day: Apple Pay in EU storefronts, and a fix for delayed order confirmations under email-provider throttling).
